Gen, this is probably going to be a longer comment and I am not writing it for anyone except for you to read, so hopefully you see it. I just had a few things to ask and to add regarding the content of this video.

- A -
We are very close to the same age. In the introduction, when you said that people watching probably only remember one crash, I wasn't thinking of COVID or early 2020s inflation. I was thinking about 2008, when my parents lost their jobs and life got really hard for a long time. Luckily, we didn't lose our house like so many other people did. But throughout the rest of the video, you didn't really talk about 2008 in terms of that 1-2-3-4 formula... only briefly about the way the market and the fed responded. If we want to pick any market crash in living memory, 2008 is the real one to look at when it comes to the hardships that followed for normal people.

- B -
I don't think the 1-2-3-4 formula accurately describes 1929 or 2008. There's a large amount of context for both of them which I don't think can be left out. The 1929 crash had a huge component of borrowed money in the 1920s, but the real cause was World War I. The United States, which had remained neutral for almost the entire war, loaned a massive amount of money to Britain and France. Britain and France, in turn, loaned a lot of that money to Russia. Imperial Russia ceased to exist in 1917, and following the Russian Civil War, the Soviet government simply opted to default on the Tsar's war debt. The Treaty of Versailles imposed huge reparations on Germany to be paid mostly to Britain and France. That money never materialized because Germany faced hyperinflation and post-war economic depression on a scale we can't even imagine today, followed by the Nazis who built their economy on unsustainable lies and defaulted on war reparations entirely. What this meant back in the U.S. was that banks looked at their lending sheets throughout the 1920s and saw nothing but green; of course they lent money freely. Everything looked great... until the moment when it became clear that the Russian and German debt was never going to be paid to Britain and France, who could then never repay their American creditors. At that point, the healthy paper balances collapsed and it took the US economy with it. Part of the reason it took so long to recover was because the Allied nations fought another world war in that time and had to rebuild the global economy to clear those debts through international economic growth rather than simple payments. I don't think it's accurate to say that 1929 was just hype over some new technology, like aircraft or radio. It wasn't like that at all. There were serious structural problems with the world economy after the Great War, and that was what finally caught up to the market in 1929. During the 1920s, European nations were already basically living in a state of economic depression.

You didn't really identify some hype technology or theme leading into 2008.... and I can't think of one that fits either. Sure, the 2000s were a party for the wealthy. But I think the real blame for the Global Financial Crisis and Great Recession lies first and foremost with the credit rating agencies, who intentionally falsified credit ratings and exposed huge parts of the U.S. economy, like pensions and retirement funds, to junk bonds and complex derivatives. Sure, wealthy investors, private capital, and the Fed stepped in to try and halt the market when it was in freefall. But by then, the damage to ordinary people was already done. The crash of the housing market should not have threatened the entire financial system and the main street economy. But it did, because perverse incentives caused the credit rating agencies to pretend that "mortgages" were gold when they knew they weren't.

The Great Depression gave us the New Deal, and the Great Recession gave us the CFPB, ACA, and Dodd-Frank. Because both of those events had systemic root cause failures, we didn't just keep on partying as if they had not been real. Whether or not certain lobbyists, wealthy Americans, and politicians willfully erode those safety nets for short-term greed does not change the fact that they were created. From a regulatory standpoint, both still strongly exist today. Am I missing something with the historical context? Even though the 1-2-3-4 formula might be catchy and seemingly evident for people who pay attention to current events, I am not convinced that they explain the two most serious crashes in the last century. Bubbles maybe, but a true economic crash is too catastrophic to be driven by careless hype alone. To be clear, I don't think that another historic crash is impossible. Just that we don't know what we don't know until we find out the hard way, and I don't know if your contemporary analysis is historically complete.

- C -
The main point of your video, which is that normal people are not insulated from market crashes, is the one to really focus on, and I think is demonstrably proven true over and over again. It is tragic that many people in our generation are unwilling to see it that way. If and when there is a market crash on the scale of the Great Depression, or even the 2008 Recession, ordinary people will be the ones to bear the pain. A quote from The Big Short sticks with me:

"If we're right, people lose homes. People lose jobs. People lose retirement savings, people lose pensions. You know what I hate about fucking banking? It reduces people to numbers. Here's a number: for every 1% that unemployment goes up, 40,000 people die. Did you know that?"

That number is true and it came from landmark research conducted by Dr. M. Harvey Brenner in the late 1970s. Who knows what the number could be today? Research conducted continuously since 2008 shows a clear depression in the lifetime earnings of young professionals, their decisions to start families, and even their life expectancy. How many graduates in 2009 were forced to take a temporarily permanent job as a bus driver because they couldn't find a career in their field? How many kids grew up in hardship during the 1920s and Great Depression only to lose their lives in WWII? These events cast long shadows over our society. The next one will be no different. Thanks for trying to drive that home, because the takes I see from many people online these days are nothing if not purely naive.

A major market crash is becoming increasingly difficult to trigger. There are several fundamental reasons behind this.

First, an enormous amount of money is now locked into the market through retirement accounts, particularly 401(k) plans. This type of institutionalized, long-term investment participation barely existed in the 1930s and was much less prevalent even in the 2000s.

Second, the growing popularity of index funds has transformed many investors who might otherwise have been active traders into passive, long-term investors. This creates a more stable investment base and potentially reduces selling pressure during market downturns.

Another factor, although perhaps less fundamental, is a change in investor psychology. Many investors have learned that market crashes are historically followed by recoveries, and timing the market is extremely difficult. While it may be relatively easy to decide when to get out because the market looks overheated, knowing when to get back in is a much harder decision. As a result, riding out a market crash may seem like a smarter strategy than attempting to time the market.

This is particularly true when we consider that some of the market's strongest returns have historically occurred during the periods surrounding major market downturns and recoveries. In fact, correctly predicting a crash but being three years too early may no longer look like a brilliant prediction.
